items.sentence_raw: Collecting must be one of the most varied of human activities, and it's one that many of us psychologists find fascinating.
Many forms of collecting have been dignified with a technical name: an arctophilist collects teddy bears, a philatelist collects postage stamps, and a deltiologist collects postcards.
Amassing hundreds or even thousands of postcards, chocolate wrappers or whatever, takes time, energy and money that could surely be put to much more productive use.
And yet there are millions of collectors around the world.
Why do they do it?
There are the people who collect because they want to make money - this could be called an instrumental reason for collecting; that is, collecting as a means to an end.
They'll look for, say, antiques that they can buy cheaply and expect to be able to sell at a profit.
items.explain: Q14: The passage says collectors look for *'antiques that they can buy cheaply and expect to be able to sell at a profit'*. This is the example given for making money. So the answer is **antiques**.

items.sentence_raw: But there may well be a psychological element, too - buying cheap and selling dear can give the collector a sense of triumph.
items.explain: Q15: The passage says buying cheap and selling dear can give a *'sense of triumph'*. A **'sense of'** something means a feeling. So the answer is **triumph**.

items.sentence_raw: And as selling online is so easy, more and more people are joining in.
Many collectors collect to develop their social life, attending meetings of a group of collectors and exchanging information on items.
items.explain: Q16: The passage says collectors attend meetings and *'exchanging information on items'*. **'Exchanging'** means sharing. So the answer is **information**.

items.sentence_raw: This is a variant on joining a bridge club or a gym, and similarly brings them into contact with like-minded people.
items.explain: Q17: The passage says joining a club *'brings them into contact with like-minded people'*. **'Like-minded'** means having similar interests. So the answer is **contact**.

items.sentence_raw: Another motive for collecting is the desire to find something special, or a particular example of the collected item, such as a rare early recording by a particular singer.
Some may spend their whole lives in a hunt for this.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says some *'spend their whole lives in a hunt for this'* special item. A **'hunt'** is a search. So the answer is **hunt**.

items.sentence_raw: Psychologically, this can give a purpose to a life that otherwise feels aimless.
items.explain: Q19: The passage says the search *'can give a purpose to a life that otherwise feels aimless'*. If a life is **aimless**, it has no direction. So the answer is **aimless**.

items.sentence_raw: There is a danger, though, that if the individual is ever lucky enough to find what they're looking for, rather than celebrating their success, they may feel empty, now that the goal that drove them on has gone.
If you think about collecting postage stamps, another potential reason for it - or, perhaps, a result of collecting - is its educational value.
items.explain: Q20: The passage says a reason for stamp collecting is *'its educational value'*. **'Educational'** means it teaches you facts. So the answer is **educational**.

items.sentence_raw: Stamp collecting opens a window to other countries, and to the plants, animals, or famous people shown on their stamps.
Similarly, in the 19th century, many collectors amassed fossils, animals and plants from around the globe, and their collections provided a vast amount of information about the natural world.
Without those collections, our understanding would be greatly inferior to what it is.
In the past - and nowadays, too, though to a lesser extent - a popular form of collecting, particularly among boys and men, was trainspotting.
items.explain: Q21: The passage says a popular form of collecting, *'particularly among boys and men, was trainspotting'*. This means it was mostly a male hobby. So the answer is **Trainspotting**.

items.sentence_raw: This might involve trying to see every locomotive of a particular type, using published data that identifies each one, and ticking off each engine as it is seen.
Trainspotters exchange information, these days often by mobile phone, so they can work out where to go to, to see a particular engine.
As a by-product, many practitioners of the hobby become very knowledgeable about railway operations, or the technical specifications of different engine types.
Similarly, people who collect dolls may go beyond simply enlarging their collection, and develop an interest in the way that dolls are made, or the materials that are used.
These have changed over the centuries from the wood that was standard in 16th century Europe, through the wax and porcelain of later centuries, to the plastics of today's dolls.
items.explain: Q23: The passage says 16th century dolls were made of *'wood that was standard'*, not wax and porcelain. Wax and porcelain came in later centuries. The question says they were normally made of wax and porcelain, which is the opposite. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: Or collectors might be inspired to study how dolls reflect notions of what children like, or ought to like.

Not all collectors are interested in learning from their hobby, though, so what we might call a psychological reason for collecting is the need for a sense of control, perhaps as a way of dealing with insecurity.

Stamp collectors, for instance, arrange their stamps in albums, usually very neatly, organising their collection according to certain commonplace principles - perhaps by country in alphabetical order, or grouping stamps by what they depict - people, birds, maps, and so on.
One reason, conscious or not, for what someone chooses to collect is to show the collector's individualism.
Someone who decides to collect something as unexpected as dog collars, for instance, may be conveying their belief that they must be interesting themselves.
items.explain: Q25: The passage says someone collecting *'unexpected'* items like dog collars may be *'conveying their belief that they must be interesting themselves'*. **'Unexpected'** means unusual, and **'interesting themselves'** means they want others to think they are unusual. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: And believe it or not, there is at least one dog collar museum in existence, and it grew out of a personal collection.
Of course, all hobbies give pleasure, but the common factor in collecting is usually passion: pleasure is putting it far too mildly.
More than most other hobbies, collecting can be totally engrossing, and can give a strong sense of personal fulfilment.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says *'More than most other hobbies, collecting can be totally engrossing, and can give a strong sense of personal fulfilment'*. This means collecting gives a feeling that other hobbies are unlikely to inspire. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: To non-collectors it may appear an eccentric, if harmless, way of spending time, but potentially, collecting has a lot going for it.

orphan_explain_map.22: Q22: The passage talks about materials used for dolls changing over centuries, but it never mentions the **number of people buying dolls**. This information is simply missing. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.

The passage does not say if arranging by size is less common. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
